attribution.note: Marcus's own characterisation in his post. The executive quote he cites is evidence, not his claim.

semantics.note: Faithful present-tense observation about Salesforce's stance. Klarna comparison correctly treated as framing.

contract.note: The plain reading (reduced trust plus reduced reliance, short of abandoning AI) is ordinary and fair. Whether 'backing down' covers adding deterministic guardrails is an interpretive point the contract flags.

evidence.note: Attributed reporting, available before the cutoff. A Salesforce SVP says trust in LLMs fell over the year, and the report says Agentforce increasingly relies on if-then rules. It also carries the company's denial.
Secondary summary dated Dec 25, 2025. It repeats the executive's remarks and the pivot to rule-based automation, plus a spokesperson's denial of backtracking. Mixed content, so context.

reviews.rationale: A named executive acknowledged lower trust in LLMs. Attributed reporting describes Agentforce shifting toward deterministic automation and limiting generative AI in some uses. That meets the support condition on the contract's reading. The only counterevidence is Salesforce's own denial, a company disclosure that does not show the reporting was wrong.

attribution.note: Marcus's own description of what the METR study showed.

semantics.note: Keeps the study as the source and the 'sometimes' qualifier.

contract.note: The contract tests what the July paper reported in its own setting, which matches his limited wording.

evidence.note: The July 2025 arXiv paper (RCT, 16 developers, 246 tasks) reports that allowing AI raised completion time by 19%.
Later METR update (Feb 2026) on a different period and setup. It restates the original slowdown and does not contradict it.

reviews.rationale: The July METR paper directly reports that AI tools slowed experienced developers by 19% in the studied setting. That satisfies 'sometimes impair productivity'. The later METR work covers different tools and a different period, so it is context only.

semantics.note: 'Betting heavily' softens 'completely smitten' but keeps 'appear', both actors and both hoped-for outcomes. It is a broad, partly rhetorical observation.

contract.note: The plain reading (substantial commitments linked to LLM-driven AGI and economic change by leading firms and the administration) is ordinary. 'Silicon Valley' and 'completely smitten' have no thresholds, so interpretation matters.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own disclosure: the Microsoft-OpenAI deal is built around AGI milestones and includes a $250B Azure commitment. Supports the corporate AGI part.
Microsoft's own earnings remarks describe AI capacity expansion at unprecedented scale. Shows heavy corporate commitment, though not tied to AGI as such.
The White House EO links AI leadership to economic dominance and a 'technological revolution'. It mentions neither LLMs nor AGI, so it does not settle the White House part.

reviews.rationale: The corporate part is supported: major firms made huge, AGI-framed LLM commitments. The support condition needs joint evidence, though, and the packet's White House records show economic-transformation goals without any LLM-to-AGI hope. Nothing contradicts the claim, but the White House part is not established, so the claim as a whole is unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus's own summary of others' findings.

semantics.note: Keeps 'many others have found' and 'not quite'.

contract.note: The plain reading (multiple groups reporting material shortfalls against promoted expectations in 2025) is fair and ordinary. 'Many' has no threshold.

evidence.note: The preliminary MIT NANDA report finds most enterprise GenAI pilots show no measurable P&L return.
Republication of Stack Overflow's July 2025 survey of 49k+ developers. Trust in AI accuracy fell to 29%, and many spend extra time fixing almost-right code.
The same survey reports productivity gains among agent users. This limits broader claims but does not negate the reported disappointment.

reviews.rationale: Several independent 2025 sources (the NANDA enterprise report, the large Stack Overflow survey) document shortfalls in returns and reliability against expectations. That meets the support condition for 'many others have found... not quite as advertised'. The benefits some users report qualify the picture without contradicting the claim.
